title: Cultivating Governance: An Exploratory Analysis of Urban Garden Management Models for Long-Term Sustainability
content: The transformation of food systems has driven the growth of urban agriculture and, in particular, community gardens as green infrastructure offering social, health and envi-ronmental benefits; however, little is known about how governance shapes these out-comes. This study analyses and compares the governance models of seven urban gardens in the Valencia Functional Urban Area (Spain) and explores their social dimensions: participation, community cohesion, inclusion and learning. A qualitative cross-sectional design with intra-method triangulation was employed, combining 10 semi-structured interviews and 5 focus groups (33 participants in total) selected through purposive sampling and analysed using thematic analysis. The allotments do not follow a single model, but rather form a continuum between community self-management and insti-tutional management, with three coexisting configurations (self-managed, institutional and hybrid), the hybrid model being the predominant one in practice. Institutional support is crucial to their survival, but only when it complements rather than replaces the community; the main vulnerability does not stem from community dynamics, but from the legal and administrative framework that subordinates allotment use to the management of public land. The social function takes precedence over the productive one. It is concluded that governance is the central mediating factor, and it is recom-mended that the complementarity of the municipal, associative and hybrid models be recognised.
